lesson.title: Strings Know Tricks: Built-in String Methods
lesson.summary: Python strings come bundled with dozens of built-in methods, invoked with dot notation, that handle common text tasks like changing case, searching for substrings, and trimming whitespace, always returning a new string rather than editing the original.
lesson.body:
Slicing and indexing let you pull characters out of a string, but plenty of everyday text tasks are awkward to build from scratch every time: removing stray whitespace from user input, converting text to all lowercase before comparing it, checking whether a sentence contains a particular word. Python strings come with a large built-in toolbox for exactly these jobs, called string methods. A method is called using dot notation, writing the string (or a variable holding one) followed by a dot, the method's name, and parentheses, as in word.upper() or sentence.strip().

Because strings are immutable, as covered in the previous section, every string method returns a brand new string rather than changing the original in place. This is worth repeating because it is the single most common source of confusion when people first start using string methods: calling sentence.lower() does nothing to sentence itself; it hands back a new lowercase string that has to be captured, either by printing it directly or by assigning it to a variable, or the result is simply thrown away.

Here are a few of the most common string methods working together:

sentence = "  Hello, World!  "
cleaned = sentence.strip()
lower = cleaned.lower()
print(cleaned)
print(lower)
print(cleaned.replace("World", "Python"))

Trace each step. sentence.strip() removes leading and trailing whitespace, the two spaces on each end, without touching whitespace in the middle, producing "Hello, World!", which is stored in cleaned. cleaned.lower() converts every uppercase letter to lowercase, producing "hello, world!", stored in lower. The first print outputs Hello, World! (the stripped version, with its original capitalization intact, since strip() only touches whitespace). The second print outputs hello, world! (fully lowercase). The third line calls .replace("World", "Python") directly on cleaned, searching for every occurrence of the substring "World" and swapping it for "Python", which produces and prints Hello, Python!, while cleaned itself remains "Hello, World!" afterward, unchanged, exactly as immutability predicts.

Beyond these three, a handful of other methods come up constantly. .startswith("He") and .endswith("!") check whether a string begins or ends with a given substring, returning True or False, which makes them a natural fit inside the flag variable and loop-else patterns from earlier in this unit. .find("World") searches for a substring and returns the index where it starts, or -1 if it is not found there at all, which is itself a sentinel value baked into the method's own design. .split() breaks a string apart into a list of pieces wherever whitespace occurs by default, which is often the very first step in processing a sentence word by word.

Because there are so many string methods, no one memorizes all of them at once, and that is fine. What is worth internalizing now is the shared pattern behind every single one: they are called with dot notation on a string, they read the string without altering it, and they return a new value, usually a new string, that has to be used or stored to matter. Once that pattern feels automatic, reaching for the right method, and looking up an unfamiliar one when needed, becomes far easier than trying to remember every method by name in advance.
